method: Each catalog row was looked up in OpenAlex, an open index of scholarly works, between 11 and 16 November 2026. Rows with DOIs were matched through every DOI in the doi field, and the reference work is the most-cited article-type record among them; dataset deposits, registry entries and front matter do not count as articles. A doi field that begins with N/A or UNVERIFIED contributes only the DOIs it labels as reference works. Rows without a usable DOI were matched on the quoted title in the citation, with a publication year within one year and the first author's surname. Without a surname, the title had to have at least five words and a similarity of at least 0.95. Of the 2,269 rows, 1,193 matched a reference article (1,177 distinct works), 302 matched only a dataset record, and 774 could not be matched. Among the unmatched rows, 447 citations have no quoted title, 321 had no acceptable candidate and 6 DOIs are not in OpenAlex. Wherever citation_count was unverified, it now carries the OpenAlex count with its source and month; 102 earlier Google Scholar counts were kept and labelled as such.

For each of the 1,177 reference works, every citing work listed in OpenAlex was collected: 334,338 rows covering 237,573 distinct citing works. Each row holds the citing work's identifier, year, type and research field, and nothing about its authors. Two datasets count as used together when a work cites both reference articles. The strength of a pair is the cosine of the two citing sets, the number of shared citing works divided by the geometric mean of the two totals. The network keeps datasets with at least 20 citing works and pairs with at least three shared citing works, which leaves 830 datasets and 11,068 pairs; catalog rows that share a reference article form a single node. Communities come from the Louvain method with a fixed seed, centrality is eigenvector centrality on the cosine weights, and bridging is betweenness on distances of one over the cosine. The drawn backbone keeps each dataset's five strongest links.
findings: The centre of the network is the regime-classification canon. The Geddes-Wright-Frantz autocratic regimes data, Cheibub-Gandhi-Vreeland, Boix-Miller-Rosato, Archigos and Svolik's authoritarian regimes data have the highest eigenvector centrality, and they lead a community of 148 datasets that also draws in historical and executive data. The UCDP/PRIO Armed Conflict Dataset and the Fearon-Laitin civil war data anchor a second community of 112 datasets, mostly conflict data together with human rights and ethnicity datasets.

Conflict and regime data are used together more than any other pair of domains (10,498 co-citations summed over dataset pairs), followed by conflict and international relations (6,726) and political economy and regimes (6,464). Conflict datasets are also the most self-contained: 38 percent of their co-citations stay inside the domain. For regional collections, data infrastructure, executives, gender, elections and historical data the share is between 1 and 7 percent, so their datasets are cited mostly alongside data from other domains.

The datasets that bridge communities are mostly regime and leader data. Boix-Miller-Rosato has the highest betweenness, followed by the Ideology of Heads of Government data, the UCDP georeferenced event data and Geddes-Wright-Frantz. Counted by citing works alone, the most-cited references lie outside political science's own canon: the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index, Global Forest Change and SPEIbase each have more than 9,000 citing works, and 39 percent of all citing works fall in OpenAlex subfields that name political science or international relations.
caveats: OpenAlex counts are a lower bound. Books, working papers and some grey literature are indexed incompletely, and citation links are missing for some publishers, so the counts often differ from Google Scholar's and from the Crossref counts quoted in row notes. Each row is credited through one reference article, the most-cited one listed in its doi field. Datasets introduced across several articles, or whose doi field omits the most-cited one or names it without calling it a reference work, are undercounted or left unverified (PARTY-033 and OPIN-115 are examples).

Co-citation records use together in the citing literature, not joint analysis: a work that reviews or criticises two datasets counts as much as one that merges them. Totals are summed over dataset pairs, so domains with many datasets accumulate larger numbers. Eigenvector centrality is computed on the largest connected part of the network, so 89 datasets outside it score zero. Only the 830 datasets with at least 20 citing works appear; rows that matched only a dataset record or could not be matched are absent.
